prompt: What causes more than half of truck driver deaths in crashes?
choices: Rear-end collisions
Railroad crossing crashes
Truck rollovers
Brake failures on downgrades
explanation: More than half of truck driver deaths in crashes are the result of truck rollovers.

prompt: Compared with empty rigs, how much more likely are fully loaded rigs to roll over in a crash?
choices: Ten times more likely
Twice as likely
Five times more likely
Equally likely
explanation: Fully loaded rigs are ten times more likely to roll over in a crash than empty rigs, because the center of gravity is higher.

prompt: What two things help most to prevent a rollover?
choices: Keep the trailer empty and use the trailer hand valve in curves
Load the heaviest cargo on top and brake in turns
Keep tires at low pressure and steer quickly
Keep cargo low and drive slowly around turns
explanation: Keep the cargo as close to the ground as possible, and drive slowly around turns.

prompt: The load in your trailer is shifted to one side so the trailer leans. What is the effect?
choices: The trailer will off-track less in turns
A rollover is more likely
The trailer brakes will lock on that side
There is no effect if the load is under the weight limit
explanation: If the load is to one side so it makes the trailer lean, a rollover is more likely. Keep cargo centered and spread out.

prompt: Where should you drive especially slowly to prevent rollovers?
choices: On straight, level interstate highways
Around corners and on ramps
Only when the trailer is empty
Only in rain, snow, or fog
explanation: Rollovers happen when you turn too fast. Drive slowly around corners, on ramps, and off ramps, and avoid quick lane changes.

prompt: What is the "crack-the-whip" effect?
choices: The jolt felt when the fifth wheel locks onto the kingpin
The trailer swinging out when its wheels lock up
The rear wheels cutting inside the path of the front wheels
A trailer tipping over from a quick steering move
explanation: In a quick lane change, the crack-the-whip effect (caused by rearward amplification) can turn the trailer over, sometimes without the tractor overturning.

prompt: What causes the crack-the-whip effect?
choices: Rearward amplification
Off-tracking of the rear wheels
Air brake lag
Trailer jackknifing
explanation: Rearward amplification causes the crack-the-whip effect, where a sudden steering move is magnified at the rear of the rig.

prompt: Triples have a rearward amplification of 3.5. What does this mean?
choices: Triples need 3.5 times the following distance of a single trailer
The last trailer off-tracks 3.5 feet farther than the first one
The last trailer rolls 3.5 times as easily as a five-axle tractor
Triples take 3.5 seconds longer to stop than a tractor-semitrailer
explanation: You can roll the last trailer of triples 3.5 times as easily as a five-axle tractor.

prompt: You make a sudden lane change while pulling doubles. Which trailer is most likely to turn over?
choices: The front trailer
Each trailer is equally likely
The tractor rather than either trailer
The rear trailer
explanation: Because of rearward amplification, the rearmost trailer is most likely to turn over in a quick lane change.

prompt: Your combination vehicle is 60 feet long and you are traveling at 50 mph. What is the minimum following distance the manual recommends?
choices: 6 seconds
4 seconds
7 seconds
3 seconds
explanation: Allow at least 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length (6 seconds for 60 feet), plus another second when going over 40 mph, for 7 seconds.

prompt: When pulling trailers, how should you steer?
choices: Quickly, to keep the trailer from drifting
Gently and smoothly
With short, firm jerks of the wheel
Only with one hand on the wheel
explanation: Steer gently and smoothly. A sudden movement of the steering wheel can tip a trailer over.

prompt: When does a large combination vehicle take longer to stop?
choices: When it is empty
When it is fully loaded
When it has ABS on all axles
It always takes the same distance
explanation: Large combination vehicles take longer to stop when empty than when fully loaded, because stiff springs and strong brakes give poor traction and the wheels lock easily.

prompt: Why does a lightly loaded combination vehicle lock its wheels so easily?
choices: Stiff springs and strong brakes give poor traction
Its brakes receive less air pressure than when loaded
Its ABS shuts off whenever the trailer is light
Its tires heat up faster than they do with a load
explanation: When lightly loaded, the very stiff suspension springs and strong brakes give poor traction, making it very easy to lock up the wheels. The trailer can swing out and the tractor can jackknife.

prompt: How does a bobtail tractor's stopping distance compare with that of a tractor-semitrailer loaded to maximum gross weight?
choices: The bobtail stops in about half the distance
The bobtail takes longer to stop
They stop in about the same distance
The bobtail stops faster on wet roads only
explanation: Tests have shown bobtails (tractors without semitrailers) can be very hard to stop smoothly and take longer to stop than a fully loaded tractor-semitrailer.

prompt: Which kind of trailer is most likely to get stuck on a raised railroad crossing?
choices: A tanker with baffles
A dry van with a sliding tandem
A lowboy or other low-slung unit
A flatbed hauling a light load of lumber
explanation: Low-slung units such as lowboys, car carriers, moving vans, and possum-belly livestock trailers can get stuck on raised crossings.

prompt: Besides low-slung trailers, which rig can get stuck on a raised railroad crossing?
choices: A tandem-axle tractor pulling a short, empty trailer with its landing gear fully raised
A bobtail tractor crossing at a sharp angle with its fifth wheel slid all the way forward
A straight truck towing a small utility trailer whose tongue jack has been removed
A single-axle tractor pulling a long trailer whose landing gear is set for a tandem-axle tractor
explanation: A single-axle tractor pulling a long trailer with its landing gear set to accommodate a tandem-axle tractor can hang up on raised crossings.

prompt: Your trailer gets stuck on railroad tracks. What should you do first?
choices: Stay in the cab and keep trying to rock the rig free
Lower the landing gear to lift the trailer
Get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks
Walk down the tracks to flag the train
explanation: If you get stuck on the tracks, get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks. Then call for help.

prompt: What tends to happen when a trailer's wheels lock up?
choices: The tractor's steering locks
The trailer stops faster and straighter
The spring brakes release
The trailer tends to swing around
explanation: When trailer wheels lock up, the trailer tends to swing around. This type of jackknife is called a trailer jackknife.

prompt: A trailer jackknife is more likely to happen when the trailer is:
choices: Empty or lightly loaded
Fully loaded
Equipped with spring brakes
Pulled by a tractor with ABS
explanation: Trailer wheel lockup and swing-out are more likely when the trailer is empty or lightly loaded.

prompt: What is the earliest and best way to recognize that your trailer has started to skid?
choices: Feeling the steering wheel shake
Seeing it in your mirrors
Hearing the air brakes release
Watching the application pressure gauge
explanation: The earliest and best way to recognize a trailer skid is by seeing it in your mirrors. Check them any time you brake hard.

prompt: Your trailer starts to skid and swing out. Why should you NOT use the trailer hand brake to straighten the rig?
choices: The hand brake works only while the rig is parked
The hand brake will release all of the tractor's brakes
The trailer brakes caused the skid in the first place
Using it will close the tractor protection valve
explanation: The brakes on the trailer wheels caused the skid. Release the brakes to get traction back; once the trailer wheels grip the road, it will follow the tractor and straighten out.

prompt: What is off-tracking (also called "cheating")?
choices: Rear wheels following a different path than the front
A trailer swinging out sideways when its brakes lock up
Drifting slowly out of your lane on a straight road
A trailer rolling over during a quick lane change
explanation: When a vehicle goes around a corner, the rear wheels follow a different path than the front wheels. This is off-tracking or cheating.

prompt: In a turn with doubles, which wheels off-track the most?
choices: The rear wheels of the tractor
The front wheels of the tractor
The rear wheels of the first trailer
The rear wheels of the last trailer
explanation: Longer vehicles off-track more, and if there is more than one trailer, the rear wheels of the last trailer off-track the most.

prompt: You can't make a right turn without entering another lane. What is the best way to turn?
choices: Swing wide to the left before starting the turn
Turn wide as you complete the turn
Turn from the left lane of a two-lane road
Let the rear wheels run up over the curb
explanation: Turn wide as you complete the turn. Swinging wide to the left before starting can invite other drivers to pass you on the right.

prompt: Why should you keep the rear of your vehicle close to the curb when turning right?
choices: To reduce how much the trailer wheels off-track
So drivers can't pass you on the right
To give pedestrians more room to cross in front
To keep the trailer from jackknifing in the turn
explanation: Steer wide enough that the rear does not run over the curb, but keep the rear close to the curb so other drivers can't pass you on the right.

prompt: When you start backing a trailer, which way do you turn the steering wheel?
choices: The same direction you want the trailer to go
Fully left, then fully right
It does not matter while backing slowly
Opposite to the way you want the trailer to go
explanation: When backing a car, straight truck, or bus, you turn the top of the wheel toward where you want to go. With a trailer, you turn the wheel in the opposite direction.

prompt: Once the trailer starts to turn while you are backing, what must you do?
choices: Turn the wheel the other way to follow it
Keep turning the wheel the same direction as before
Stop and pull out the trailer air supply knob
Speed up so the trailer straightens out on its own
explanation: Once the trailer starts to turn, you must turn the wheel the other way to follow it.

prompt: If you must back a trailer on a curved path, which way should you back?
choices: Toward the passenger side, to protect the cab
Either side, using only the right mirror
Toward the driver's side, so you can see
In a straight line first, then turn blind-side
explanation: Try to back in a straight line. If you must back on a curved path, back to the driver's side so you can see.

prompt: While backing, your trailer begins to drift off the proper path. How do you correct it?
choices: Turn the top of the wheel away from the drift
Apply the trailer hand valve to stop the drift
Stop, then reset the fifth wheel slide position
Turn the top of the wheel toward the drift
explanation: As soon as you see the trailer getting off the proper path, correct it by turning the top of the steering wheel in the direction of the drift.

prompt: What does the manual recommend if you are unsure of your path while backing a trailer?
choices: Rely on the right-side mirror only
Back faster to finish before traffic arrives
Get out and re-inspect your path
Sound the horn and keep backing
explanation: Check the mirrors on both sides often, and get out of the vehicle to re-inspect your path if you are unsure. Back slowly and use pull-ups as needed.

prompt: What is the trailer hand valve (trolley valve or Johnson bar) meant to be used for?
choices: Slowing the rig on downgrades
Only to test the trailer brakes
Parking the trailer
Straightening a skidding trailer
explanation: The trailer hand valve should be used only to test the trailer brakes. Using it while driving risks a trailer skid.

prompt: Why should you never use the trailer hand valve to park?
choices: The air may leak away and let the trailer roll
It holds the fifth wheel jaws in the open position
It drains the tractor's air tanks within seconds
It applies only the brakes on the tractor
explanation: All the air might leak out and unlock the brakes on trailers without spring brakes. Always use the parking brakes, and chock trailers without spring brakes.

prompt: What does the tractor protection valve do?
choices: Saves the tractor's air if the trailer breaks away
Keeps the tractor from jackknifing on wet or icy roads
Limits the air pressure sent to the tractor's front brakes
Keeps the fifth wheel jaws locked around the kingpin
explanation: The tractor protection valve keeps air in the tractor or truck brake system should the trailer break away or develop a bad leak.

prompt: The tractor protection valve closes automatically when air pressure falls into what range?
choices: 55 to 60 psi
20 to 45 psi
80 to 85 psi
100 to 125 psi
explanation: The tractor protection valve closes automatically when air pressure is low, in the range of 20 to 45 psi.

prompt: When the tractor protection valve closes, what happens to the trailer?
choices: Its service brakes release and it rolls freely behind you
It keeps braking normally using air from the tractor's tanks
Its emergency line is vented, so its emergency brakes come on
Its ABS takes over and pumps the brakes automatically
explanation: When the valve closes it stops air from leaving the tractor and lets the air out of the trailer emergency line, causing the trailer emergency brakes to come on, with possible loss of control.

prompt: On newer vehicles, what does the trailer air supply control look like?
choices: A yellow, diamond-shaped knob
A round blue knob
A green, square button
A red, eight-sided knob
explanation: The trailer air supply control is a red eight-sided knob. The yellow diamond knob is the parking brake control.

prompt: What happens when you pull out the trailer air supply knob?
choices: The trailer is supplied with air so you can drive away
The tractor's spring brakes are released for driving
Trailer air is shut off and its emergency brakes come on
The fifth wheel locking jaws open so the trailer can be dropped
explanation: Push the knob in to supply the trailer with air; pull it out to shut the air off and put on the trailer emergency brakes.

prompt: What two air lines run between each vehicle in a combination?
choices: The primary line and the secondary line
The pressure line and the return line
The parking line and the relay line
The service line and the emergency line
explanation: Every combination vehicle has two air lines, the service line (also called the control or signal line) and the emergency line (also called the supply line), running between each vehicle.

prompt: What controls the air in the service line?
choices: The foot brake or the trailer hand brake
The trailer air supply knob on the dash
The governor on the air compressor
The tractor protection valve by itself
explanation: The service line (also called the control or signal line) carries air controlled by the foot brake or the trailer hand brake. Pressure varies with how hard you apply them.

prompt: What does the service line connect to on the trailer that helps the trailer brakes apply quickly?
choices: The safety relief valve
Relay valves
The tractor protection valve
The shut-off valves
explanation: The service line is connected to relay valves, which allow the trailer brakes to be applied more quickly than would otherwise be possible.

prompt: What are the two purposes of the emergency (supply) line?
choices: It powers the trailer lights and the ABS malfunction lamp
It applies the service brakes and releases the parking brakes
It fills the trailer tanks and controls the emergency brakes
It drains the trailer tanks and cools the brake drums
explanation: The emergency line supplies air to the trailer air tanks and controls the emergency brakes. Loss of pressure in it causes the trailer emergency brakes to come on.

prompt: Your trailer breaks loose and tears the emergency air hose. What happens?
choices: Trailer emergency brakes come on; the tractor protection valve closes
The trailer rolls freely until you press the service brake pedal
Only the tractor's front brakes are applied, by the limiting valve
The tractor's air tanks empty out through the broken hose
explanation: Loss of pressure in the emergency line puts on the trailer emergency brakes and causes the tractor protection valve to close (the air supply knob pops out).

prompt: What color is commonly used to mark the emergency air line?
choices: Blue
Yellow
Green
Red
explanation: Emergency lines are often coded red, and service lines blue, to keep them from getting mixed up.

prompt: What are glad hands?
choices: Hand grips used to climb up onto the tractor's deck
Couplers for the trailer's service and emergency air lines
Gloves worn when checking and pulling slack adjusters
Latches that lock the fifth wheel jaws around the kingpin
explanation: Glad hands are coupling devices used to connect the service and emergency air lines from the truck or tractor to the trailer.

prompt: How do you connect a pair of glad hands?
choices: Line them up end to end and push them until they click
Press the seals together at 90 degrees, then turn to lock
Screw them together clockwise until they are hand-tight
Clamp them side by side using a standard hose clamp
explanation: Clean the couplers and seals, press the two seals together with the couplers at a 90-degree angle, and turn the glad hand attached to the hose to join and lock them.

prompt: What should you do to the glad hand couplers and rubber seals before connecting them?
choices: Grease them
Remove the seals
Spray them with alcohol
Clean them
explanation: Clean the couplers and rubber seals before a connection is made; the seals prevent air from escaping.

prompt: You crossed the air lines when coupling a trailer that has spring brakes. What will you notice?
choices: The trailer spring brakes won't release
The trailer brakes work normally, just a little more slowly
The low air warning comes on as soon as you start the engine
The tractor's own spring brakes come on immediately and lock
explanation: With crossed lines, supply air goes to the service line instead of charging the trailer tanks, so there is no air to release the trailer spring brakes. Check the air line connections.

prompt: Why are crossed air lines especially dangerous on an older trailer without spring brakes?
choices: The trailer brakes would lock and drag the whole trip
The tractor protection valve would never close
You could drive away with no trailer brakes at all
The trailer lights would stop working
explanation: If the trailer air tank has leaked down and the lines are crossed, you could drive away but have no trailer brakes. Always test the trailer brakes before driving.

prompt: What are dummy (dead-end) couplers used for?
choices: Testing the trailer brakes before you drive away
Connecting a second trailer to the first trailer
Releasing the trailer spring brakes in an emergency
Storing unused hoses to keep water and dirt out
explanation: Dummy couplers hold the hoses when they are not in use, preventing water and dirt from getting into the coupler and air lines. It is very important to keep the air supply clean.

prompt: Your trailer air tanks have automatic drains. What should you still do?
choices: Nothing; automatic drains never need checking
Drain them only once a month
Open the drains to make sure moisture is removed
Add alcohol to each tank daily instead
explanation: Drain each tank every day. Automatic drains keep most moisture out, but you should still open the drains to make sure.

prompt: What is another name for shut-off valves on trailers?
choices: Glad hands
Cut-out cocks
Relay valves
Johnson bars
explanation: Shut-off valves, also called cut-out cocks, are used in the service and supply lines at the back of trailers used to tow other trailers.

prompt: In a set of doubles, which air line shut-off valves should be closed?
choices: Only the ones at the back of the last trailer
The ones at the back of the first trailer only
All of the shut-off valves on the dolly
The ones at the front of every trailer
explanation: All shut-off valves must be open except the ones at the back of the last trailer, which must be closed.

prompt: Which units are NOT required to have spring brakes?
choices: Converter dollies and trailers built before 1975
Trailers built on or after March 1, 1998
Any trailer that is equipped with working ABS
Trailers that are longer than 48 feet in length
explanation: Newer trailers have spring brakes, but converter dollies and trailers built before 1975 are not required to have them.

prompt: You park a trailer that has no spring brakes. Why must you chock its wheels?
choices: Its spring brakes may overheat and release overnight
Its brakes hold only until the tank air leaks away
Its parking brake works only while the engine is running
Its ABS releases the brakes after a few minutes parked
explanation: Trailers without spring brakes have no parking brake; their emergency brakes hold only while there is air in the trailer tank. Eventually the air leaks away, leaving no brakes.

prompt: Your trailer has a major leak in the service line. When are you likely to notice it?
choices: As soon as you start the engine
Only during the pre-trip leakage test with brakes released
When you put on the brakes and tank pressure drops quickly
When the trailer ABS lamp lights up
explanation: You may not notice a major service line leak until you apply the brakes. Then the air loss lowers tank pressure quickly, and if it goes low enough the trailer emergency brakes come on.

prompt: Trailers and converter dollies are required to have ABS if they were built on or after:
choices: March 1, 1997
January 1, 1994
January 1, 1975
March 1, 1998
explanation: All trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998 must have ABS. (Air-braked truck tractors were required from March 1, 1997.)

prompt: Only your trailer has ABS. During hard braking, the tractor starts to jackknife. What should you do?
choices: Keep full brake pressure, since the trailer ABS will fix it
Apply the trailer hand valve to pull the tractor straight
Let up on the brakes, if safe, until you regain control
Pull out the trailer air supply knob right away
explanation: With ABS only on the trailer, the trailer is less likely to swing out, but if you lose steering control or start a tractor jackknife, let up on the brakes (if safe) until you regain control.

prompt: Which statement about driving a combination with ABS is true?
choices: ABS lets you follow more closely in good weather conditions
ABS lets you take curves at a higher speed than normal
ABS means you no longer need to plan to brake early
ABS won't let you drive faster or follow more closely
explanation: ABS won't allow you to drive faster, follow more closely, or drive less carefully. Brake as you always have.

prompt: Why must the fifth wheel plate be greased as required?
choices: Lack of grease can cause steering problems from friction
Grease keeps the kingpin from locking too tightly in the jaws
Grease keeps air from leaking out of the glad hand seals
Grease keeps the landing gear legs from rusting
explanation: Failure to keep the fifth wheel plate lubricated could cause steering problems because of friction between the tractor and trailer.

prompt: Before coupling, what position should the fifth wheel be in?
choices: Tilted up toward the cab, with the jaws closed
Tilted down toward the rear, with the jaws open
Level with the frame, with the jaws closed and locked
Tilted down toward the cab, with the jaws open
explanation: The fifth wheel should be tilted down toward the rear of the tractor, jaws open, and the safety unlocking handle in the automatic lock position.

prompt: Why should you never back under a trailer at an angle?
choices: The glad hands would cross each other automatically
The trailer's ABS malfunction lamp would come on and stay on
It can push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear
The kingpin would lock onto the outer edge of the jaws
explanation: Put the tractor directly in front of the trailer. Backing under at an angle might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear.

prompt: When coupling, how high should the trailer be?
choices: Low enough that the tractor lifts it slightly
High enough that the fifth wheel clears it completely
Exactly level with the top of the fifth wheel plate
Resting on the ground at the front, below the kingpin
explanation: The trailer should be low enough that it is raised slightly by the tractor when backed under it.

prompt: What can happen if the trailer is too high when you try to couple?
choices: The tractor will strike and damage the trailer nose
The landing gear will collapse
The air lines will cross
It may not couple correctly
explanation: If the trailer is too high, it may not couple correctly. If it is too low, the tractor may strike and damage the trailer nose.

prompt: During coupling, after supplying air to the trailer, why do you shut the engine off?
choices: So the air tanks can fill up more quickly
So you can hear the trailer brakes work
So the tractor protection valve can reset itself
So the fifth wheel jaws can close on the kingpin
explanation: Shut the engine off so you can hear the brakes. When you apply and release the trailer brakes, you should hear them move and hear air escape on release.

prompt: How do you do the tug test to check the coupling?
choices: Release the trailer brakes and back up hard against the kingpin
Pull gently forward with the trailer brakes locked
Pull forward quickly with the landing gear still down
Drive around the yard at 15 mph and then brake hard
explanation: Raise the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground, then pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked to check that the trailer is locked on.

prompt: Before going under the trailer to inspect the coupling, why should you shut off the engine and take the key?
choices: So the air tanks can bleed down for the next test
So the fifth wheel jaws have time to close fully
So the trailer spring brakes will release on their own
So no one moves the truck while you're under it
explanation: Put the transmission in neutral, set the parking brakes, shut off the engine, and take the key so someone else won't move the truck while you are under it.

prompt: After coupling, how much space should there be between the upper and lower fifth wheel?
choices: None
About 1 inch
About 2 inches
About one-half inch
explanation: There should be no space between the upper and lower fifth wheel. If there is space, the kingpin may be on top of the closed jaws and the trailer could come loose.

prompt: You see a gap between the upper and lower fifth wheel after coupling. What might be wrong?
choices: The fifth wheel plate needs more grease
The trailer air tanks have not been charged yet
The kingpin may be on top of the closed jaws
The landing gear has been raised too high
explanation: A gap means something is wrong: the kingpin may be on top of the closed fifth wheel jaws, and the trailer would come loose very easily.

prompt: When you look into the back of the fifth wheel, what should the jaws be closed around?
choices: The head of the kingpin
The upper fifth wheel plate
The release handle
The shank of the kingpin
explanation: Make sure the fifth wheel jaws have closed around the shank of the kingpin, not the head.

prompt: You find the coupling isn't right during your inspection. What should you do?
choices: Drive slowly to the nearest shop
Drive normally and recheck at the next stop
Don't drive the coupled unit; get it fixed
Add grease and continue
explanation: If the coupling isn't right, don't drive the coupled unit. Get it fixed.

prompt: When raising the landing gear after coupling, which gear range do you use?
choices: High range to start, then low range near the very top
Low range first, then high range once it's free of weight
High range the whole way, since it is faster
Low range the whole way, stopping when it is halfway up
explanation: Use the low gear range (if equipped) to begin raising the landing gear, then switch to high once it is free of weight. Raise it all the way.

prompt: During uncoupling, why do you back up gently and set the parking brakes while the tractor pushes against the kingpin?
choices: To take pressure off the locking jaws
To lock the trailer brakes before its air is shut off
To lower the landing gear down onto the ground
To check that the trailer is still coupled tightly
explanation: Backing gently eases pressure on the fifth wheel locking jaws, and setting the parking brakes while pushing holds the rig with pressure off the jaws, making the release lever easier to pull.

prompt: When uncoupling a loaded trailer, what should you do after the landing gear makes firm contact with the ground?
choices: Give the crank a few extra turns in low gear
Raise the trailer completely off the fifth wheel
Stop cranking right away so the landing gear does not bend
Keep lowering the gear until the tractor's rear tires lift
explanation: With a loaded trailer, a few extra turns in low gear lift some weight off the tractor, making it easier to unlatch and to couple next time. Don't lift the trailer off the fifth wheel.

prompt: When you first pull the tractor out from under the trailer during uncoupling, where should you stop?
choices: Fully clear of the trailer
With the tractor frame still under the trailer
With the fifth wheel still under the kingpin
About 10 feet past the trailer's nose
explanation: Stop with the tractor frame under the trailer. This keeps the trailer from falling to the ground if the landing gear collapses or sinks.

prompt: While pulling the fifth wheel release handle, what should you keep clear of the rear tractor wheels?
choices: The air lines
The electrical cord
Your legs and feet
The wheel chocks
explanation: Keep legs and feet clear of the rear tractor wheels to avoid serious injury in case the vehicle moves.

prompt: During uncoupling, when should you chock the trailer wheels?
choices: Only if the trailer is loaded with cargo
Only when parked on a downhill grade
Never, since the trailer brakes are always enough
If it lacks spring brakes, or you aren't sure
explanation: Chock the trailer wheels if the trailer doesn't have spring brakes or if you are not sure. Air could leak from the trailer tank and release its emergency brakes.

prompt: When coupling a gooseneck trailer, what should you attach after latching the coupler clamp over the ball?
choices: The safety chains
The landing gear crank handle
The trailer hand valve line
The fifth wheel safety latch
explanation: After positioning the coupler over the ball and latching the clamp, attach the safety chains, then connect the trailer light wiring and check all lights, including brake lights.

prompt: During a walk-around, which is a defect in the lower fifth wheel?
choices: Locking jaws closed around the shank of the kingpin
No visible space between upper and lower fifth wheel
Release arm seated with the safety latch engaged
Locking jaws closed around the head of the kingpin
explanation: The locking jaws must be around the shank, not the head, of the kingpin. No visible space and an engaged safety latch are correct.

prompt: When inspecting the air lines to the trailer, what should you look for?
choices: Proper connection, no leaks, and slack for turns
Lines pulled tight so they cannot move around
Lines resting flat on the fifth wheel plate
Service and emergency lines taped together as one
explanation: Air lines should be properly connected to the glad hands, have no air leaks, and be properly secured with enough slack for turns. All lines should be free of damage.

prompt: What should you check on the landing gear during a walk-around?
choices: Lowered halfway so uncoupling will be quicker
Fully raised, undamaged, crank handle secured
Crank handle removed and stored inside the cab
Resting lightly on the pavement for support
explanation: Landing gear should be fully raised with no missing, bent, or damaged parts, the crank handle in place and secured, and no leaks if power operated.

prompt: To check that air flows to all trailers, what do you do at the rear of the last trailer?
choices: Pull the trailer air supply knob and watch the ABS lamp
Disconnect the glad hands and listen for escaping air
Open the emergency line valve and listen for air
Drain the last trailer's air tank all the way down
explanation: With the trailer air supply knob pushed in and the hand brake applied, open the emergency line valve at the rear of the last trailer and listen for air, then do the same for the service line. Close the valves afterward.

prompt: During the air flow check, you hear no air from the rear shut-off valves. What should you check?
choices: That the trailer and dolly shut-off valves are open
That the governor cut-out pressure is above 140 psi
That the trailer ABS malfunction lamp is working
That the landing gear is raised all the way up
explanation: If you do not hear air escaping from both lines, check that the shut-off valves on the trailer(s) and dolly(ies) are open. You must have air all the way to the back.

prompt: How do you test the tractor protection valve?
choices: Engine running, pull out the air supply knob and drive forward
Disconnect the service line and listen for escaping air
Open the tank drains with the engine running at fast idle
Engine off, fan the brakes until the air supply knob pops out

prompt: How do you test the trailer emergency brakes?

Pull the air supply knob out and gently pull against it
Shut off the engine and listen for any air leaks at the trailer
Disconnect the electrical cord, then drive slowly forward

Roll forward slowly and use the trailer hand control
Set the tractor parking brake while rolling forward
Back up slowly and press the foot brake firmly

prompt: If the tractor protection valve does not work right, what could happen?

The governor would never let the compressor cut in
A trailer leak could drain all the tractor's air

prompt: Why must you raise the trailer landing gear all the way before driving?

prompt: When backing the tractor under the trailer to couple, which gear should you use?

Neutral, letting the tractor coast back on a slight grade
The lowest reverse gear, backing slowly
Any reverse gear, with the trailer brakes released
explanation: Use the lowest reverse gear and back slowly under the trailer to avoid hitting the kingpin too hard. The trailer brakes should be locked, and you stop when the kingpin locks into the fifth wheel.

prompt: After unplugging the trailer electrical cable during uncoupling, how should you hang it?

With the plug facing up
Coiled on the fifth wheel plate
Tied to the trailer's landing gear
